candidates.attacker_control: Indirect: the request rate/timing and concurrency of callers invoking methods annotated with @RateLimit (or configured via the Guard/TypedGuard programmatic API). Configuration values (value/window/minSpacing/type) come from application configuration/annotations, not directly from remote input.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Configuration is validated in RateLimitConfig.validate() (value >= 1, window >= 1, minSpacing >= 0) and in the programmatic builders (FaultToleranceImpl lines 807-829, GuardImpl 626-648, TypedGuardImpl 720-748), so zero/negative configuration is rejected before enforcement; all visible TimeWindow.record() implementations are synchronized and cap permits. RateLimitEvents, RateLimitLogger and RateLimitException exist and are consistent with a strategy class that was simply excluded from the snapshot. The absence of the files may be a dataset/packaging artifact and is not runtime-confirmed as a defect.
candidates.impact: If the missing enforcement class is weak or bypassable (or fails open on a negative/overflowed retry-after value), the rate limiting control that bounds request rates would not bound resource consumption, enabling resource-exhaustion/denial-of-service against the guarded application. Impact is inferred from the missing enforcement point; it is not demonstrated by any visible code path in this snapshot.
candidates.prerequisites: A rate limit configured declaratively or programmatically; an attacker able to invoke the guarded method at high volume. The referenced enforcement class must be absent/broken for a real bypass to exist - that precondition cannot be checked in this snapshot.
candidates.root_cause: The only class that consumes the TimeWindow implementations and decides whether an invocation is permitted or rejected - io.smallrye.faulttolerance.core.rate.limit.RateLimit - is missing from the source tree, as is the api.RateLimit annotation source. Five visible call sites construct `new RateLimit<>(...)` (FaultToleranceInterceptor 428-435 and 506-513, FaultToleranceImpl 327-334 and 405-412, GuardImpl 257-264, TypedGuardImpl 257-264) and the annotation is used by FaultToleranceMethods, FaultToleranceExtension, RateLimitConfig and FaultToleranceMethod, yet no definition exists. Because enforcement is entirely delegated to that absent class, any weakness in its apply()/record()/RateLimitException construction (permit/deny decision, retry-after handling, or rejection bookkeeping) is invisible in this snapshot and cannot be verified; no other visible component enforces the configured limit.
candidates.title: Rate-limit enforcement implementation is absent from the snapshot, so the enforcement/decision path for all @RateLimit / Guard rate limits cannot be reviewed
candidates.trace: FaultToleranceInterceptor.prepareStrategy()/prepareFutureStrategy() wraps the invocation chain in `new RateLimit<>(result, point.toString(), operation.getRateLimit().value(), timeInMillis(window...), timeInMillis(minSpacing...), type, SystemStopwatch.INSTANCE)` (lines 428-435, 506-513); FaultToleranceImpl.buildSyncStrategy/buildAsyncStrategy (327-334, 405-412), GuardImpl.buildStrategy (257-264) and TypedGuardImpl.buildStrategy (257-264) do the same. The visible TimeWindow implementations (FixedWindow, SmoothWindow, RingBufferRollingWindow) only return a retry-after value from record(); the absent core RateLimit class is the sole place that converts that value into PERMITTED/REJECTED and a RateLimitException. RateLimitException (api, lines 23-78) has no producer anywhere else in the snapshot, confirming enforcement is solely in the missing class.
candidates.unverified: The primary evidence is a definition absence, not an observed weakness: `RateLimit.java` (core) and `RateLimit.java` (api) do not exist in the snapshot although many files import/reference them, so no vulnerable logic could actually be read or traced. No build, tests or runtime checks were performed; no request was ever shown to bypass a rate limit. Line ranges for the two absent files are inferred (1-120 / 1-60) and are not backed by file content.
candidates.weakness_type: Suspected ineffective security control / rate-limit enforcement not verifiable (CWE-693, potentially CWE-770)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 270 files (235 Java, 35 non-Java) under the assigned root; 0 files excluded by path/name/size/symlink filters and 0 binary-skip detections, per get_source_scope. Relation index: 270/270 files indexed, 0 parse errors, no omitted files; relations are syntactic name/containment/call/inheritance candidates only (no control/data flow, no semantic resolution, no Spring/DI runtime verification, 3051 unresolved calls). I read/inspected the core strategies (Bulkhead, CircuitBreaker + rolling windows, Timeout/FutureTimeout, Retry/back-off/jitter, all rate-limit window classes, Future/FutureImpl/Completer, ThreadTimer), the CDI interceptor and extension, config validation and FaultToleranceOperation/Methods, programmatic Guard/TypedGuard/FaultTolerance builders and EventHandlers, metrics providers/recorders, SecurityActions reflection paths, context-propagation/tracing/vertx adapters, standalone configuration, autoconfig annotation processor, and the CI/pom files. Not fully line-by-line reviewed: metrics recorder internals, Kotlin/Mutiny/RxJava async-support adapters, and parts of the very large apiimpl classes beyond the strategy-building sections named above.
limitations: Two files that are imported/referenced throughout the tree are missing from the snapshot: implementation/core/src/main/java/io/smallrye/faulttolerance/core/rate/limit/RateLimit.java and api/src/main/java/io/smallrye/faulttolerance/api/RateLimit.java. The rate-limiting enforcement logic therefore could not be read at all; the candidate is an inference from the missing enforcement point plus its call sites, not from observed code.
The relation index was built over the same 270-file snapshot, so it contains no symbols/edges for the missing classes either; the index proves nothing about runtime reachability or exploitability.

No build, tests, scanners or runtime execution were performed; no runtime confirmation of any candidate. The snapshot would not compile as-is because of the missing referenced classes, which also prevents any static build-based verification.

No patch, fix commit, CVE metadata, sibling condition or ground-truth data was inspected (per instructions), so the intended weakness for this case could not be cross-checked; the missing-file pattern is the basis of the lead.
CI workflow and pom files were only skimmed; metrics recorder implementations and Kotlin/Mutiny/RxJava adapter code were not exhaustively reviewed.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultAsyncExecutorProvider (implementation/fault-tolerance, lines 43-57): mainThreadPoolQueueSize=1 silently falls into the else branch and creates an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue even though the validation message says the value must be -1, 0 or >1; a developer expecting a bound of 1 gets unbounded queueing (potential memory exhaustion).
rejected_leads.reason: Concrete but low-severity configuration-handling mismatch; the configured value 1 is arguably invalid, the queue is still bounded by maxSize worker threads and callers would need heavy async load, and it is not connected to the absent rate-limit files that dominate this case's evidence. Kept as an unconfirmed secondary lead, not submitted.

rejected_leads.lead: config/SecurityActions.setAccessible and fault-tolerance/SecurityActions use AccessController.doPrivileged to force-reflectively access fallback/before-retry methods (FaultToleranceOperation lines 91-123), which bypasses accessibility and CDI interceptor-based security checks on those methods.
rejected_leads.reason: This is the documented design of MicroProfile Fault Tolerance fallback/before-retry invocation and matches upstream code; no attacker-controlled class/method name or privilege escalation was identified. Not a demonstrable vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: ThreadTimer keeps scheduled timer tasks in a ConcurrentSkipListSet and the async executor/timer can be fed by retry/timeout scheduling; a flood of configured retries could grow scheduled tasks.
rejected_leads.reason: Task count is tied to in-flight invocations already bounded by other strategies/bulkhead; no unbounded attacker-controlled growth was traced, and the code removes tasks on run/cancel.

rejected_leads.lead: CI workflows use floating action refs (@main for smallrye/.github and radcortez/project-metadata-action) and pass the Sonar token via -Dsonar.login=$SONAR_TOKEN on the command line.
rejected_leads.reason: Supply-chain/config hygiene concerns in .github workflows; no repository source vulnerability and outside the code-level review scope.

summary:
Repository is SmallRye Fault Tolerance 6.8.1-SNAPSHOT. Review focused on the CDI interceptor/strategy chain, core fault-tolerance strategies (bulkhead, circuit breaker, timeout, retry, rate limit windows), programmatic Guard/TypedGuard builders, config validation generated from annotations, metrics providers, and reflection/SecurityActions paths.

Single strongest lead: the rate-limiting enforcement class `io.smallrye.faulttolerance.core.rate.limit.RateLimit` (and the `io.smallrye.faulttolerance.api.RateLimit` annotation) are referenced by five and fifteen-plus source files respectively, but neither file exists in the snapshot (only the annotation-based config wrapper, builder implementations, events, exception and the three TimeWindow implementations are present). All rate-limit construction sites therefore point at an implementation that cannot be inspected, while the remaining code contains no alternate enforcement point for permitted/rejected decisions. This is reported as a candidate lead only; it is not confirmed, and it may be a snapshot/packaging artifact rather than a defect. No other visible file contained a finding that met the evidence threshold.
